builder_plan.scenario: Your inference service slows down when several customers send requests together.
builder_plan.change: Replay a recorded request trace with only the proposed serving policy changed.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current scheduler on the same model and hardware.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Requests meeting your latency target, throughput, failures, and cost per successful request.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Held While Waiting: What LLM Agent Sessions Reserve on Serverless and Agent Runtimes
summary: The technique replaces the default one-reserved-environment-per-conversation model on serverless agent runtimes with explicit client-side session closing and, where the platform permits, multiplexing many conversations onto one environment; it replaces implicit 15-minute idle holds after a conversation ends. Closing costs only client-side lifecycle logic, while sharing costs platform support (largely unavailable in surveyed runtimes) and adds up to ~40 ms queuing delay for most replies; compute-per-reply figures of 5–40 ms are estimates the authors flag as hard to measure. Sharing can fail on isolation: environments hold model-selected tool and code execution, so multiplexing without adequate sandboxing risks cross-conversation leakage, and on platforms without sharing support, unclosed sessions will still exhaust the environment pool before CPU does.
rationale: Closing agent sessions explicitly at conversation end is a client-side change with no infrastructure prerequisite that directly releases the binding resource (reserved environments) on runtimes like Bedrock AgentCore.
technique: Session closing and environment multiplexing for agent runtimes

claims.statement: The technique replaces the default one-reserved-environment-per-conversation model on serverless agent runtimes with explicit client-side session closing and, where the platform permits, multiplexing many conversations onto one environment; it replaces implicit 15-minute idle holds after a conversation ends. Closing costs only client-side lifecycle logic, while sharing costs platform support (largely unavailable in surveyed runtimes) and adds up to ~40 ms queuing delay for most replies; compute-per-reply figures of 5–40 ms are estimates the authors flag as hard to measure. Sharing can fail on isolation: environments hold model-selected tool and code execution, so multiplexing without adequate sandboxing risks cross-conversation leakage, and on platforms without sharing support, unclosed sessions will still exhaust the environment pool before CPU does.

In the authors' simulation, multiplexing 64 conversations per environment reduces required environments 59-fold, with 99 of 100 replies delayed by at most 40 ms; separately, sessions are held 15 minutes after a 33-second average conversation unless the client closes them.
